---
title: "Water pollution and treatment chemistry exercises"
---

Use the values given; do not look up other constants. Predict the direction of change before calculating.

## 1. Another sequence

Two stages each remove 30.0% of the entering water-phase mass. Start with 100 mg. Find final water mass and overall removal.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Multiply the two remaining fractions.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
100 × 0.700² = **49.0 mg** remains; **51.0%** is removed from the water. The element still resides in the specified residual stream unless transformed/exported elsewhere.
:::

## 2. Coagulant acidity

Assume 0.0200 mmol/L Fe³⁺ undergoes the supplied hydroxide precipitation reaction completely. Calculate H⁺ generation and the equivalent alkalinity decrease.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Each mole Fe³⁺ produces three moles H⁺ in this representation.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
H⁺ = **0.0600 mmol/L**; alkalinity decreases by **0.0600 meq/L**. Other reactions and species must be included for a real dosing calculation.
:::

## 3. Track nitrogen

A process changes 1.00 mmol/L NH₄⁺ into 1.00 mmol/L NO₃⁻, with no other nitrogen products. Has it removed nitrogen? What process could remove dissolved nitrogen as gas?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Compare nitrogen atoms across forms.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
No: **1.00 mmol N/L** remains. Nitrification changes form. Denitrification to N₂ can export nitrogen from water, subject to the donor, conditions, and gas-transfer boundary.
:::

## 4. Choose and justify

A water contains suspended clay, dissolved nitrate, and a neutral organic contaminant. Explain why filtration alone is not a complete treatment argument.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Match particle size and chemical form to mechanism.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
Filtration can capture some particles depending on the medium and size, but dissolved nitrate and a molecular organic solute generally require other suitable mechanisms. Consider nitrate transformation/separation and contaminant-specific sorption or destruction, then account for residuals and products. No operating prescription follows from this generic example.
:::

## Explore: where the phosphorus goes {#explore}

Predict how much of 100 mg phosphorus reaches the effluent if three stages
transfer 30 %, 40 % and 90 % of what enters each one. Is it 100 − 160 %? Then
change one stage at a time and watch where the removed phosphorus ends up.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../demos/demo.css">
<div data-demo="treatment" role="group" aria-label="Sequential treatment stages and the phosphorus mass balance">
<p>Reference case: 100 mg phosphorus through stages transferring 30 %, 40 % and 90 % of what enters each leaves 4.2 mg (4.2 %) in the effluent; 30.0 + 28.0 + 37.8 = 95.8 mg is in sludge.</p>
</div>
<script src="../demos/core.js"></script>
<script src="../demos/treatment.js"></script>
```

**E1.** Choose **Phosphorus plant**. Check the three sludge amounts and the
effluent by hand, then show that the four parts add up to 100 mg. Why is the
"added percentages" value impossible?

**E2.** Choose **Exercise 1** and compare with your answer to exercise 1. Then
set stage 3 to 50 %. Does a third stage of 50 % halve the overall removal, or
the amount left in the water?

**E3.** In the phosphorus plant, which single stage would you improve by 5
percentage points to lower the effluent most? Try each one. Then explain why the
sludge total rises by exactly the amount the effluent falls.

### Model conditions and hand check

Each stage transfers a fixed fraction of the mass that **enters it** to sludge;
there is no gas or chemical-product stream, which suits phosphorus and metals but
not nitrogen. The stage percentages are round constructed numbers, not data from
a real plant. For the reference case, the fraction left is
0.70 × 0.60 × 0.10 = 0.042, so **4.2 mg** of 100 mg reaches the effluent and
**95.8 %** is transferred: 30.0 mg, 0.40 × 70.0 = 28.0 mg and
0.90 × 42.0 = 37.8 mg to sludge. The notes' worked example (10.0 mg, 60.0 %
then 50.0 %) gives 2.00 mg in the effluent and 80.0 % overall. Nothing is
destroyed: the sludge still has to be managed.
